TITLE: Investigating Scaling Limits of Pretraining for DPT
PROPOSAL: Implement a set of controlled experiments that scale up DPT pretraining from the current discrete-action environments to a synthetic multi-domain collection of continuous-control tasks with distinct MDP structures. Specifically, we will: (1) utilize a synthetic dataset with continuous-control tasks that vary in MDP dimensionality (e.g., Cart-Pole, Mountain-Car, Double Pendulum) and reward structures; (2) pretrain the DPT model with a fixed cross-entropy loss on the offline data under various settings (number of environment domains, task instances per domain, maximum sequence length); and (3) analyze the pretraining process' impact on the DPT model's ability to capture complex continuous action posteriors, eg22 Native sampling efficiency, and generalization to unseen tasks.
CONTROLS: Vanilla DPT with fixed maximal sequence length, vanilla DPT with fixed number of environment domains.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (approximate, assuming a batch size of 128 and 16 GB V100 GPUs).
PREDICTION: We expect that increasing the number of domains or task instances per domain during pretraining will improve the model's generalization to unseen tasks but that further scaling (e.g., too many environments or long sequences) may lead to diminishing returns or even deteriorating performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating Action Distribution Models for DPT
PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare several action distribution models for DPT that can effectively capture complex continuous action posteriors in diverse environments, including: (1) parallel sigmoid families (e.g., diNet) for modeling localized continuous actions; (2) gan-like generators for modeling high-dimensional continuous distributions; and (3) mixture models (e.g., Gaussian mixture models) that can adapt to varying task characteristics. This will involve modifying the DPT architecture to incorporate these different action distribution models and evaluating their performance in terms of native action sampling efficiency and generalization to unseen tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline DPT model with a simple standard normal distribution over actions, ablation across the different action distribution models to assess their impact on performance.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (approximate, assuming batch size of 128, 16 GB V100 GPUs, and multiple DPT model variants to train).
PREDICTION: We anticipate that more expressive action distribution models, such as the gan-like generator and the mixture model, will significantly improve DPT's generalization to diverse environments, but may incur a slight penalty in terms of native action sampling efficiency.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Investigating Transferability of DPT In-Context Learning to Novel Tasks and Environments
PROPOSAL: Evaluate DPT's in-context learning capabilities by adding novel tasks and environments to the pretraining setup, investigating how effectively the model can adapt to these new scenarios through conditional actions provided at test time. Specifically, we will: (1) augment the offline dataset with a selection of novel tasks and environments drawn from the synthetic dataset (e.g., a novel robotic manipulation scenario or an off-road driving environment); (2) evaluate whether DPT can adapt to these novel tasks using shortest prompts, and analyze the prompt length and contextual knowledge's impact on performance; (3) study the benefits of reinforcement learning from human illustrations (RLHF) and a text-based 'rule-of-thumb' provided at test time to improve adaptability.
CONTROLS: assess baseline in-context learning in absence of text-based 'rule-of-thumb', investigate impact of prompt quality and length.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (approximate, assuming batch size of 128, 16 GB V100 GPUs and multiple novel scenarios to test).
PREDICTION: We expect that in-context learning will demonstrate value for adapting to novel tasks, particularly when combined with RLHF and rule-of-thumb knowledge. However, we anticipate varying levels of transferability based on the similarity of the novel tasks to those seen during pre-training.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Efficient and Interpretable Action Sampling for DPT
PROPOSAL: Investigate and develop new, efficient and interpretable methods for action sampling in DPT that align with the Bayesian posterior sampling interpretation. Specifically, we will: (1) explore approximate Bayesian inference techniques (e.g., variational inference, gradient-based methods) to improve the computational efficiency of action sampling; (2) investigate the use of learned, task-specific action sampling distributions that capture the structures present in the action space; and (3) study the benefits of leveraging the learned context-dependent action posteriors as prior knowledge to guide sample-efficient search.
CONTROLS: Baseline DPT action sampling via random or uniform sampling, ablate the effect of using pretraining-generated context-dependent action posteriors on efficiency and performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (approximate, assuming batch size of 128, 16 GB V100 GPUs and multiple DPT model variants to train).
PREDICTION: We expect that these more efficient action sampling methods will improve DPT's performance in terms of generalization and real-time adaptability, particularly when combined with pretraining-generated context-dependent action posteriors. However, we anticipate that their interpretability may be compromised.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Meta-Domain Generalization: Training DPT for Exotic and Dynamic Environments
PROPOSAL: Investigate and develop methods to train DPT for the meta-domain scenario where the model must preadapt to unseen domains and adapt to entirely new, exotic, or dynamic reality-like environments during deployment. Specifically, we will: (1) mimic meta-domain scenarios by adversarially creating a variety of offline datasets with varying environment dynamics during pretraining; (2) use metrics assessing domain shift and performance across novel domains as training objectives; and (3) leverage self-aware decision-making strategies for dynamically allocating compute resources within the inference pipeline to handle changes in domain characteristics.
CONTROLS: Baseline DPT model trained on a single MDP environment, evaluate the effect of self-aware decision-making on redirecting compute resources when domain changes.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (approximate, assuming batch size of 128, 16 GB V100 GPUs, and online generation of meta-domain scenarios via environment simulations).
PREDICTION: We expect that self-aware decision-making and preadaptation techniques will improve DPT's robustness and adaptability in meta-domain scenarios, but variable pretraining environments and dynamics might influence efficiency and real-time response.

TITLE: Unifying Offline and Online Learning for Scalable Generalization
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework for learning the DPT model that combines the benefits of offline pretraining and online adaptation, leveraging both datasets to learn a robust, generalizable policy. TITLE: Meta-Implicit Shaping for In-Context Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel meta-implicit shaping mechanism to reinforce the Decision Pretrained Transformer (DPT) with task-specific cues, encouraging the model to implicitly learn to adapt to unseen tasks and exploit prior knowledge more effectively. This is achieved by modeling the implicit shaping objective as a set of meta-learned task-specific priors that are learned from a diversity of demonstration datasets. The meta-implicit shaping objective can be integrated with the existing Bounded Mixture-Of-Experts Architecture for Continuous Action Inference and Meta-Exploration via In-Policy Parameter-sharing for Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts, effectively augmenting the model's ability to leverage high-level task information and generalize to new tasks.

PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-task meta-reinforcement learning approach that learns to adapt to a variety of tasks concurrently, while leveraging the benefits of in-context learning. This approach will be based on the Decision Pretrained Transformer (DPT) architecture, and will incorporate the meta-implicit shaping mechanism to provide task-specific cues.
